articles.title: La furia di Putin su Kiev e Leopoli, due missili cadono in Polonia
articles.summary: La Nato in allerta. Mosca valuta una visita degli E3, Trump vuole la pace entro gennaio
articles.preview: Vladimir Putin aveva promesso una "risposta dolorosa" ai raid di Kiev contro il Ponte di Crimea. Meno di 24 ore dopo, le forze russe hanno sferzato l'Ucraina con una serie di massicci attacchi che nella notte hanno preso di mira tre ponti a Kiev dove sei persone sono rimaste uccise, e hanno raggiunto anche Leopoli e le regioni dell'ovest provocando due vittime.
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin aveva promesso una "risposta dolorosa" ai raid di Kiev contro il Ponte di Crimea. Meno di 24 ore dopo, le forze russe hanno sferzato l'Ucraina con una serie di massicci attacchi che nella notte hanno preso di mira tre ponti a Kiev dove sei persone sono rimaste uccise, e hanno raggiunto anche Leopoli e le regioni dell'ovest provocando due vittime.

Una salva di morte e distruzione che stavolta ha sconfinato anche in Polonia, dove è stata segnalata la caduta di due missili nel territorio sudorientale del Paese, uno dei quali - stando al Telegraph - esploso a 96 km dal luogo in cui si stanno svolgendo esercitazioni militari dei Volenterosi. Una circostanza per la quale Donald Tusk è incline a escludere la coincidenza fortuita: "Apparentemente ci troviamo di fronte a una provocazione intenzionale".

"Questa non è solo una mia valutazione, ma anche quella dei nostri partner stranieri, compresi quelli della Nato: non sembra un incidente", ha affermato il leader di Varsavia. Le autorità hanno confermato che un missile è caduto nel villaggio orientale di Nowy Lipowiec, mentre si sospetta che un altro missile e un drone a reazione abbiano colpito due ulteriori località. Varsavia ha reso noto che non vi sono stati feriti, ma intanto la tensione é salita alle stelle: Tusk ha informato "immediatamente" la Nato che nella notte ha fatto alzare i suoi jet.

"Questo incidente è chiaramente pericoloso", ha sottolineato il segretario Mark Rutte, professando "unità come alleati" continuando a "sostenere l'Ucraina". I missili in Polonia infiammano le tensioni che passano anche dalla Danimarca, dove il governo ha espulso l'addetto alla difesa dell'ambasciata russa a Copenaghen e ha minacciato sospendere il rilascio di visti Schengen per i cittadini russi, accusando Mosca di essere coinvolta nel tentato omicidio di un rapper ucraino.

"Invece di mostrare la volontà di impegnarsi in colloqui di pace, Mosca continua a diffondere le proprie minacce e a concretizzare questi attacchi contro gli Stati membri dell'Unione europea", ha denunciato il presidente del Consiglio europeo, Antonio Costa, dando voce allo scetticismo dell'Ue nei confronti del Cremlino all'indomani dell'invito a Mosca di Vladimir Putin ai leader europei: il viceministro degli Esteri Serghei Ryabkov ha specificato che la proposta dello zar era rivolta ai Paesi dell'E3 ed "è una possibilità che stiamo attualmente prendendo in considerazione".

Ma al momento, non si trova una risposta comune: dopo che il cancelliere tedesco Friedrich Merz ha chiesto di riunirsi in un "luogo neutrale", l'Eliseo ha aperto all'incontro a Mosca solo se gli europei avranno il loro posto a pieno titolo nei negoziati. In questo quadro, la pioggia di missili e droni russi non aiuta il fragile percorso diplomatico per chiudere la guerra.

"Putin ha lanciato un attacco molto eclatante dopo incontri deboli in Cina e il fallimento del suo tentativo di 'redistribuire' il mondo", è la lettura di Volodymyr Zelensky. Se da una parte l'Ucraina è stata la grande assente dalla 'dichiarazione di pace' tra Putin, Trump e Xi (una 'clausola inappropriata' sarebbe stata rimossa dal testo su richiesta Usa) dall'altra lo storico trilaterale a Shenzhen ha spinto il tycoon a contattare gli alleati europei per chiarire che 'l'amico' Vladimir Putin "vuole mettere fine alla guerra, vuole che l'accordo sia concluso e si sta stancando di questa situazione", stando a quanto riferito da Axios.

Secondo il Financial Times che cita quattro fonti, il presidente americano si è posto l'obiettivo di raggiungere un accordo di pace entro l'inizio di gennaio, prima che i Democratici assumano il controllo del Congresso. Una tempistica che ha accresciuto le preoccupazioni che il presidente Zelensky possa essere costretto ad accettare un accordo alle condizioni di Mosca. Le indiscrezioni parlano ancora di una possibile cessione di territori in cambio dell'adesione ucraina alla Nato, o a un meccanismo simile all'Articolo 5. Ma "la probabile adesione di Kiev all'Alleanza è uno dei motivi della guerra", ha ricordato il superfalco di Putin, Dmitry Medvedev. Al netto delle intenzioni, la strada per la pace resta in salita.

articles.body:
An Indian man was sentenced to more than 19 years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York City, in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.

Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

The US district judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a hearing in a Manhattan federal court.

The discovery of alleged assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India, which has denied involvement in such plots.

Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in New York who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.

Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.

Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired a defense lawyer.

India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.

Prosecutors with the Manhattan US attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.

“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”

Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the non-violent example set by the Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.

“I’m sorry to Mr Pannun, I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta said.

Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.

“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

articles.body:
Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.

“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,”, Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days.

“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he added.

Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.

Rasmussen also said that Denmark was considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians.

“We have launched work at the European level to further tighten the rules governing access of Russian nationals to Europe,” he said. “We are now stepping up our efforts towards a halt to all non-essential visas.

“The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine. And we fully intend to continue supporting Ukraine.”

Police thwarted the alleged plot when they arrested three men with links to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Viktorovich Vasiliev, was due to perform at a concert on 25 September, which was then cancelled, officials said. Vasiliev holds US and Ukrainian nationality.

Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, the head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, said: “It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian intelligence services.”

According to prosecutors, the suspects were driving towards the concert venue north of Copenhagen with two loaded pistols and two knives when police arrested them at about 9.55pm, five minutes before the concert was due to begin. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening, police said.

One of the suspects had bought a ticket to the concert, according to the charges.

The suspects are charged under Section 108 of Denmark’s criminal code, which covers assisting a foreign intelligence service, as well as attempted murder. They denied wrongdoing in court, the broadcaster DR reported.

Kieffer-Kristensen said: “A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and risk-taking Russia.

“We believe that the case is important for understanding the threat that Denmark faces from Russia.”

articles.summary: AGI - La sua folta capigliatura canuta e un intercalare reso celebre da un ormai altrettanto celebre fuori onda , e consacrato dall'imitazione di Maurizio Crozza , sono piuttosto familiari ai telespettatori. Ora Antonio Razzi vuole tornare in politica, questa volta in prima persona, tanto da annunciare “voglio fare un partito online per e con i giovani". "Lo chiamo ' Movimento del Terzo Millennio ', mi propongo come saggio per insegnare ai ragazzi come si fa politica", spiega l'ex parlamentare - per tre legislature, due alla Camera e poi al Senato, dal 2006 al 2018 - che sempre a Un Giorno da Pecora su Rai Radio1 gioca tra 'provocazione' e realtà: "Quando lo fondo? Antonio Razzi: "Con Tajani ho un rapporto pessimo" “Potrebbe essere che alla prima uscita prendiamo il 3%, chissà”, butta lì. Quanto al rapporto con il segretario del suo ex partito, FI, (dove arrivò lasciando Di Pietro e Idv) Razzi dice che è “ pessimo ". "Scrissi a Tajani che volevo candidarmi alle Europee per dare una mano e lui non mi ha mai risposto. Inevitabile un accenno alla politica estera, grande passione di Razzi: “Il vertice tra Xi, Trump e Putin ? articles.title: Six Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza, civil defence says
articles.summary: Six Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza, civil defence says Israeli strikes killed six people in the Gaza Strip on Friday, the civil defence agency in the war-shattered territory told AFP, despite a ceasefire. Mahmoud Bassal, the spokesman for Gaza's civil defence agency, said that four Palestinians were killed and several others wounded in an Israeli airstrike southwest of Bureij refugee camp in the central Gaza Strip on Friday. The civil defence also said one Palestinian was killed in an Israeli drone strike targeting a tent in the Al-Munasara camp for displaced people in Deir al-Balah. Another person was killed in a drone strike north of Nuseirat refugee camp, also in the central Gaza Strip. The Israeli military told AFP it had "targeted multiple military operatives" in several strikes, which came a day after the army said it had completed a ground incursion in the central Gaza Strip. More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Gaza health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. Report by AFP

articles.title: Vance refuses to endorse Iran strikes despite pressure from Trump
articles.summary: Vance refuses to endorse Iran strikes despite pressure from Trump US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to stop it developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping Trump’s calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again. Speaking at a White House press conference alongside Trump, Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February had been the president’s call, “and my job is to support the president of the United States”. After the midterm elections, Vance blamed the war for the Republicans’ historic losses and called for the US to exit the conflict. His statement, posted on social media, was widely seen as a break with Trump as the vice president weighs a 2028 White House bid. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote . “The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay.” Trump said on Friday that he was not unhappy with Vance’s conclusion but that it lacked a crucial element: an acknowledgement that the strikes were necessary and that Vance would make the same decision. “People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion,” Trump said. “But I say, I know the Iranians, and, frankly, they’re crazy.” Vice President JD Vance on Iran: "The goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It's the biggest state sponsored terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or God forbid they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands potentially, of innocent people. The president is the one who makes the decision and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the President of the United States." — Vice President JD Vance (@VP) November 20, 2026

articles.title: Inside the Iraqi Kurdish city caught between the US and Iran
articles.summary: Inside the Iraqi Kurdish city caught between the US and Iran Submitted by Sean Mathews on Fri, 11/20/2026 - 19:37 Sulaymaniyah is reeling from the economic toll of the Iran war and grappling with an emboldened regional power next door A market in the city of Sulaymaniyah in Iraq's Kurdistan Region is said to be the largest bazaar in the region, on 11 November 2026 (Sean Mathews/MEE) Off If US President Donald Trump has his way, Baran* will be out of business. The thirty-year-old Kurd is a trader who buys diesel in Iraq and sells it in Afghanistan. It’s a stressful gig, but one that can generate a tidy profit in a place like Iraqi Kurdistan. A truck laden with $20,000 worth of diesel in Iraq can sell in Kabul for around $24,000, leaving around $2,000 for the trader once expenses are paid. But it has to make it through Iran first. “The journey is more dangerous now. It’s harder to find drivers. The border isn’t as reliable. The price of diesel has also shot up,” Baran, whose name has been changed to protect his identity, told Middle East Eye. Trump says instead of restarting strikes on Iran, he wants to choke its economy. In addition to a naval blockade, the US is pressing countries like Turkey , Iraq and Pakistan to seal their borders with Iran. Earlier this month, the US announced a task force to blockade trade across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea. Baran has no political beef with the US. On the contrary, he says, “George W. Bush overthrew Saddam Hussein. He helped Kurdistan. I don’t prefer Iran to the US,” he said over a glass of anise-flavoured Arak and hookahs at a restaurant in Sulaymaniyah. “But this war has not been good for business or our economy.” Baran is a microcosm of the city he calls home. Sulaymaniyah Nestled in the Zagros Mountains, Sulaymaniyah is Iraqi Kurdistan’s second largest city. Its beating heart is a sprawling bazaar where locals boast that any item a shopper desires can be procured. November is pomegranate season, and the fruit was plentiful. The label “Made In Iran” on packages and wrappings was also ubiquitous. Sulaymaniyah prides itself on being more libertine than its rival Erbil. In the bazaar, more women go without a headscarf than with one. “If people have $50 in their pockets, they will spend it to go out here,” Baran said. Bazaar merchants flick the city’s famed prayer beads, made of pistachio tree seeds, and tea boys run around keeping everyone well caffeinated. On the surface, the vibrant bazaar gives an impression of prosperity, but the opposite is true. “The price of food is unbearable for most people now. For some products, the increase is 200 percent,” Evin*, a 28-year-old shopper, complained to MEE. “We used to import so much from Iran, but now they aren’t exporting.” Another young professional said they had to delay purchasing a new laptop computer because the price had shot up from $600 to $800 since the war started. Because of taxes and logistics, Sulaymaniyah’s most competitive trade corridor to China runs through Iran. The region has a plethora of border posts that are more convenient than the Iraqi port of Basra - which feels a world away from here - or Turkey. Goods coming from the latter are also subject to higher taxes from Turkey and Erbil. “In Iraqi Kurdistan, trade with Iran is a major part of the local economy,” Dlawer Ala’Aldeen, the president of the Middle East Research Institute, a Kurdish think-tank in Erbil, told MEE. The US-Israeli war on Iran is taking a toll across the region. The economies of all the Arabian Gulf states are expected to shrink this year. Their pitches as tourism and business hubs are in jeopardy. This month alone, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund headquarters and the tower housing state-oil company Aramco in Riyadh came under attack from the Houthis. But Iraqi Kurdistan is a unique case. 'Living on a thin margin' The region is convulsed by an internal political fissure that experts say could increase the sway of outside powers, particularly Turkey and Iran. This semiautonomous region of Iraq also lacks the deep pockets of Arab Gulf states to cushion geopolitical blows. The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has been plagued by financial difficulties for years. The region is supposed to receive around 15 percent of Iraq’s federal budget, more than 90 percent of which comes from oil revenue. Despite the war on Iran, Iraq exported more oil this month than at any time since 2019, but payments to the KRG are late. Government employees are receiving their salaries months behind schedule. The rising costs of the Iran war have only compounded the pain. Vehicles drive at the Iraq-Iran border crossing of Bashmagh near Sulaimaniyah in Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, on 11 March 2026 (AFP) Iran has deep trade ties across Iraq and the Kurdistan Region. But Sulaymaniyah is particularly close to its eastern neighbour. The city was founded in 1784 under the Baban Emirate, which controlled parts of modern-day Iraq and Iran. Many founding Kurdish families hail from across the border. “Slemani was already living on a thin margin,” Ala’Aldeen said, adding that the local economy depends on “cross-border trade, business, daily labour, and goods” from Iran. “The war did not create that fragility; it exposed it: when Hormuz closed and when the United States pressed Iraq to close all but two crossings with Iran, Slemani felt it in prices and availability of goods,” he said. “Cutting Iran off will leave Slemani without many alternatives.” Those trade ties are more interesting when one considers the pressure Iraq’s Kurdistan Region came under to join in the US-Israeli war on Iran earlier this year. An estimated 40 million Kurds live between Syria, Iraq, Turkey and Iran. Although they never got a country when the Middle East was carved up by European colonial powers, Iraqi Kurdistan gained a high degree of autonomy in the 21st century because of the support it received from the US after the US invasion of Iraq. For more than 20 years, Peshmerga fighters have been key American allies, most recently against the Islamic State militant group. The KRG also hosts some Iranian-Kurdish opposition groups who are backed by the US and Israel. When the Trump administration and Israel decided to attack Iran, they turned to Iraq’s Kurds to support opposition groups and fight across the border, but that plan never fully materialised. 'Impossible position to be in' The KRG is dominated by two family dynasties, the Barzani family in Erbil, which leads the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), and the Talabani family in Sulaymaniyah, which leads the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK). In the 1990s, Iraq’s Kurds fought a civil war which saw the PUK receive support from Iran, and the KDP from Turkey. Because of its geography and economy, Sulaymaniyah continues to be viewed as closer to Iran, so much so that Bafel Talabani, the PUK leader, denied a reporter's question at a conference earlier this month in Sulaymaniyah, put to him that he was in Iran’s “pocket”. In reality, both the PUK and KDP are closely aligned with the US. Female members of the Iranian Kurdish opposition Komala party carry the body of a Peshmerga fighter in the autonomous Kurdistan region, on 16 April 2026 (AFP) Among American officials, Bafel Talabani is known to enjoy hanging out with former American Joint Special Operations Command fighters, better known as “JSOC guys”. His brother, Qubad, the deputy prime minister of Iraqi Kurdistan, is married to a former State Department official. A former US intelligence official told MEE that the PUK was actually seen by members of the Trump administration as more receptive to plans to support Kurdish opposition groups in Iran because it was lobbying for greater attention in Washington. The PUK's territory in the KRG also shares a longer border with Iran. The PUK was courting the Trump administration in part over frustration that its rival, the KDP, had greater access in Washington as a result of controlling the Kurdistan region’s presidency. The tensions between the two parties have erupted into a major political rift that experts say risks splitting the KRG. Talabani withdrew the PUK from the region's parliament in November and told a forum in Sulaymaniyah that the KRG was already living “the reality of two governments and two administrations”. In the end, neither the PUK nor KDP joined the US war effort. A decision that many Kurds welcomed. "Kurdistan was right to refuse to be embroiled in this war. A collapse in Tehran would not arrive as a clean handover. It would arrive as chaos on Kurdistan's longest border: refugees, armed factions, a power vacuum, and a fight over who controls Iranian Kurdistan," Ala’Aldeen at the Middle East Research Institute, told MEE. Internal politics are at play now, too. Bafel Talabani is courting members of Baghdad’s ruling Shia Coordination Framework for an upper hand against the KDP. The Shia Coordination Framework is aligned with Tehran. The Kurdistan Region is also militarily exposed. It lacks proper air defence systems. The last US troops left Erbil, the region's capital, in September, completing a full US withdrawal from Iraq. The region faced hundreds of Iranian missile and drone strikes during the war. “Bafel Talabani is an ambitious guy. He speaks with everyone, too. He’s pragmatic. But he faces a very difficult position. He is seeking US support, but Iran sees Sulaymaniyah as its backyard. It’s an impossible position to be in,” Oral Toga, a senior researcher at the Centre for Iranian Studies in Ankara, told MEE. 'Iran has the upper hand' At a strategic forum hosted in Sulaymaniyah earlier this month, PUK officials emphasised their desire for dialogue and partnership with Iran. Bafel Talabani himself said that Iran had emerged “stronger but different” from the US-Israeli war and criticised those who characterise the country as being run by “mad mullahs”. Recounting a recent trip he made to Iran, he offered a very different assessment to that proposed by members of the Trump administration who have characterised Iran as on the verge of economic collapse. "I thought I was in London," Talabani said, noting that "less than 50 percent of ladies and girls had scarves" and that restaurants were filled with young people dancing. This overview shows Iraq's northeastern city of Sulaymaniyah in the autonomous Kurdistan region at sunset, on 18 October 2024 (AFP) Tehran is now pressuring Iraqi Kurdistan to clamp down on Kurdish opposition groups. In a meeting in September with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Bafal Talabani promised not to allow Iraqi Kurdistan to become "a haven for harming or threatening" the Islamic Republic. "As an ally of Mr Trump and, strangely, an ally of the Iranians [I say] the mighty US can [talk to Iran],” he said at the forum. “The region feels Iran has a strategic upper hand at the moment. It’s not just Iraqi Kurdistan, but the Gulf states too. They all want to avoid Iran’s wrath," Sarhang Hamasaeed, an independent Middle East analyst, told MEE. “But Iran has shown that in this fight it isn’t factoring those relations in. Iraq has been the economic lungs of Iran, but Iran didn’t spare their exports through Hormuz," he added. Given its land border with Iran, Sulaymaniyah is even more vulnerable to reprisals should the war resume. "The Kurds in Iraq were Iran's target practice in prior years, well before Iran's war with the US and Israel. They know, and don't want to be on the receiving end of Iranian strikes," Hamasaeed said. “Between the US and Iran, they have to appease Iran more, because Trump won’t strike them with drones and missiles - Iran will,” he said. The US will not fire missiles at Iraqi Kurdistan like Iran, but America's foreign policy could endanger the region. Many in Sulaymaniyah believe the US will not be content until it collapses the Iranian government. Trump himself said as much on a radio show this month. When asked by a radio host whether he would consider it a “defeat” for him if the Islamic Republic was still in power at the end of his term, Trump said “absolutely”. "The worst thing for Sulaymaniyah and Iraqi Kurdistan would be a failed state across the border. We need stability," a Kurdish official in the city told MEE. Many founding Kurdish families hail from across the border. “Slemani was already living on a thin margin,” Ala’Aldeen said, adding that the local economy depends on “cross-border trade, business, daily labour, and goods” from Iran.

“The war did not create that fragility; it exposed it: when Hormuz closed and when the United States pressed Iraq to close all but two crossings with Iran, Slemani felt it in prices and availability of goods,” he said. “Cutting Iran off will leave Slemani without many alternatives.” Those trade ties are more interesting when one considers the pressure Iraq’s Kurdistan Region came under to join in the US-Israeli war on Iran earlier this year.

An estimated 40 million Kurds live between Syria, Iraq, Turkey and Iran. Although they never got a country when the Middle East was carved up by European colonial powers, Iraqi Kurdistan gained a high degree of autonomy in the 21st century because of the support it received from the US after the US invasion of Iraq. For more than 20 years, Peshmerga fighters have been key American allies, most recently against the Islamic State militant group.

The KRG also hosts some Iranian-Kurdish opposition groups who are backed by the US and Israel. When the Trump administration and Israel decided to attack Iran, they turned to Iraq’s Kurds to support opposition groups and fight across the border, but that plan never fully materialised. 'Impossible position to be in' The KRG is dominated by two family dynasties, the Barzani family in Erbil, which leads the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), and the Talabani family in Sulaymaniyah, which leads the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).

In the 1990s, Iraq’s Kurds fought a civil war which saw the PUK receive support from Iran, and the KDP from Turkey. Because of its geography and economy, Sulaymaniyah continues to be viewed as closer to Iran, so much so that Bafel Talabani, the PUK leader, denied a reporter's question at a conference earlier this month in Sulaymaniyah, put to him that he was in Iran’s “pocket”. In reality, both the PUK and KDP are closely aligned with the US.

Female members of the Iranian Kurdish opposition Komala party carry the body of a Peshmerga fighter in the autonomous Kurdistan region, on 16 April 2026 (AFP) Among American officials, Bafel Talabani is known to enjoy hanging out with former American Joint Special Operations Command fighters, better known as “JSOC guys”. His brother, Qubad, the deputy prime minister of Iraqi Kurdistan, is married to a former State Department official.

A former US intelligence official told MEE that the PUK was actually seen by members of the Trump administration as more receptive to plans to support Kurdish opposition groups in Iran because it was lobbying for greater attention in Washington. The PUK's territory in the KRG also shares a longer border with Iran. The PUK was courting the Trump administration in part over frustration that its rival, the KDP, had greater access in Washington as a result of controlling the Kurdistan region’s presidency.

The tensions between the two parties have erupted into a major political rift that experts say risks splitting the KRG. Talabani withdrew the PUK from the region's parliament in November and told a forum in Sulaymaniyah that the KRG was already living “the reality of two governments and two administrations”. In the end, neither the PUK nor KDP joined the US war effort. A decision that many Kurds welcomed.

"Kurdistan was right to refuse to be embroiled in this war. A collapse in Tehran would not arrive as a clean handover. It would arrive as chaos on Kurdistan's longest border: refugees, armed factions, a power vacuum, and a fight over who controls Iranian Kurdistan," Ala’Aldeen at the Middle East Research Institute, told MEE. Internal politics are at play now, too. Bafel Talabani is courting members of Baghdad’s ruling Shia Coordination Framework for an upper hand against the KDP.

The Shia Coordination Framework is aligned with Tehran. The Kurdistan Region is also militarily exposed. It lacks proper air defence systems. The last US troops left Erbil, the region's capital, in September, completing a full US withdrawal from Iraq. The region faced hundreds of Iranian missile and drone strikes during the war. “Bafel Talabani is an ambitious guy. He speaks with everyone, too. He’s pragmatic.

But he faces a very difficult position. He is seeking US support, but Iran sees Sulaymaniyah as its backyard. It’s an impossible position to be in,” Oral Toga, a senior researcher at the Centre for Iranian Studies in Ankara, told MEE. 'Iran has the upper hand' At a strategic forum hosted in Sulaymaniyah earlier this month, PUK officials emphasised their desire for dialogue and partnership with Iran.

Bafel Talabani himself said that Iran had emerged “stronger but different” from the US-Israeli war and criticised those who characterise the country as being run by “mad mullahs”. Recounting a recent trip he made to Iran, he offered a very different assessment to that proposed by members of the Trump administration who have characterised Iran as on the verge of economic collapse. "I thought I was in London," Talabani said, noting that "less than 50 percent of ladies and girls had scarves" and that restaurants were filled with young people dancing.

This overview shows Iraq's northeastern city of Sulaymaniyah in the autonomous Kurdistan region at sunset, on 18 October 2024 (AFP) Tehran is now pressuring Iraqi Kurdistan to clamp down on Kurdish opposition groups. In a meeting in September with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Bafal Talabani promised not to allow Iraqi Kurdistan to become "a haven for harming or threatening" the Islamic Republic.

"As an ally of Mr Trump and, strangely, an ally of the Iranians [I say] the mighty US can [talk to Iran],” he said at the forum. “The region feels Iran has a strategic upper hand at the moment. It’s not just Iraqi Kurdistan, but the Gulf states too. They all want to avoid Iran’s wrath," Sarhang Hamasaeed, an independent Middle East analyst, told MEE. “But Iran has shown that in this fight it isn’t factoring those relations in.

Iraq has been the economic lungs of Iran, but Iran didn’t spare their exports through Hormuz," he added. Given its land border with Iran, Sulaymaniyah is even more vulnerable to reprisals should the war resume. "The Kurds in Iraq were Iran's target practice in prior years, well before Iran's war with the US and Israel. They know, and don't want to be on the receiving end of Iranian strikes," Hamasaeed said.

“Between the US and Iran, they have to appease Iran more, because Trump won’t strike them with drones and missiles - Iran will,” he said. The US will not fire missiles at Iraqi Kurdistan like Iran, but America's foreign policy could endanger the region. Many in Sulaymaniyah believe the US will not be content until it collapses the Iranian government. Trump himself said as much on a radio show this month.

When asked by a radio host whether he would consider it a “defeat” for him if the Islamic Republic was still in power at the end of his term, Trump said “absolutely”. "The worst thing for Sulaymaniyah and Iraqi Kurdistan would be a failed state across the border. We need stability," a Kurdish official in the city told MEE. articles.body:
Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

“We want them to build it here.”

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”

He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”

Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”

He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”

And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

articles.body:
The US president also spoke about the war in Iran and praised trip to China during a wide-ranging news conference.

United States President Donald Trump has praised his recent trip to China and defended the relationship with his “friend” Vladimir Putin, but questioned whether the Russian president was a friend to the US.

On Friday, during a White House news briefing, Trump was asked about the “friend” remark — made during his historic summit with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier this week — and whether the Russian leader was a friend to the US.

“I can’t speak to America,” Trump told reporters before saying Putin had been “very nice” during what he described as the “Russia hoax” investigation after his 2016 presidential campaign.

“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship. And it’s actually very good,” Trump added as he talked about Russia’s nuclear weapons capabilities.

“I think it gives us a lot of additional strength,” he said.

Trump also spoke about the historic nature of his meeting with Xi and Putin, praising the “first of its kind trilateral peace agreement”. He said there was “great electricity” between the leaders of the world’s main nuclear powers.

“We had one of the most momentous international summits in many years. That was the first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China,” Trump said.

“I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that,” he also said.

No major deals were announced from the summit. But Trump, on Friday, played up his agreement with the two leaders to hold future discussions on nuclear proliferation.

The US president’s remarks came during a wide-ranging news conference, where topics from Iran to artificial intelligence were also discussed.

Trump accused Iran of negotiating in bad faith to end the war, which is about to mark its 10-month anniversary.

“They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me,” he said. “We wanna make a real deal, not a fake deal.”

Trump added: “They’ve been b*********** people for 51 years.”

During the news conference, US Vice President JD Vance and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, both possible 2028 presidential contenders, flanked Trump in the White House press briefing room.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Defence Secretary Hegseth, as well as newly minted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, were also present.

Trump denied he was upset at Vance for blaming US Republicans’ historic midterm losses on the Iran war, saying, “People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion.”

“I thought his statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that, if we were asked, I would have said that, would you do it again, and absolutely the answer is yes,” Trump said. “I saw that, but no problem there at all.”

No data centres abroad

Vance was asked by reporters about his thoughts on his party’s midterm drubbing.

“I think the president is the one who makes the decision. And the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said. “My goal, in my job, is to support the President of the United States.”

Trump also warned US tech companies against building new artificial intelligence data centres overseas. Otherwise, he said, they will face a “tremendous tax”.

“We’re not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them”, Trump said. “And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”

Trump did not provide details on how he would enforce such a policy and said he had not yet told his own officials about his plan.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment but has not yet heard back.

articles.preview: Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition request In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.
articles.body:
In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

Speaking outside Madrid’s Aranjuez prison upon his release on Friday, Chambers called the charges against him “baseless”, adding that his release was “hopefully the first step in recognizing that internationally”.

Chambers also said: “Spain is a country that has stood on the right side of this most important issue of our time, that has stood on the right side of the genocide, and where this is some reason and some justice.”

An appeals court ordered the conditional release on Friday due to issues surrounding the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported on by the Guardian. He had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.

The order asserts that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”.

Chambers’s release follows a separate decision on Thursday by the three-judge panel at the high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

The Guardian detailed four examples of the alterations on 7 November and the US admitted to tampering with the translation, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent” on 17 November – and citing the same four examples. Chambers’s defense team has asserted for weeks that there are as many as 30 such alterations.

The changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian earlier this week. The judges must consider the prosecutor’s report in deciding on the extradition request.

The high court was expected to rule on the extradition this week, following a 13 November hearing. But as of Thursday’s decision, the deadline has been extended indefinitely as the judges evaluate the translation, including a 345-page report submitted by the defense team that identifies 30 “incriminating changes” Trump administration officials made to a translation prepared by DeepL, “an AI-first translation platform”, according to its website.

The decision also gives the prosecutor an opportunity to address the issue in writing, after dismissing it in the 13 November hearing by referring to “supposed translation errors”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”

The heir to $250m from his family’s business, Cox Enterprises, is being sought in extradition because of such views, his defense team has asserted throughout the case.

Meanwhile, the Irish Garda Síochána, acting on a request from US authorities, raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and Schnabel on Wednesday, destroying the front door and removing electronic items and other possessions, according to their attorney in Ireland, Ciarán Mulholland.

Schnabel, who is five months pregnant, said: “It is difficult to see this raid as anything other than a desperate fishing expedition by the US authorities to find evidence to bolster their case against Fergie.”

The attorney told the Guardian that the raid was the result of a “mutual legal assistance” request from the US – and that such a request “wouldn’t give [the Garda Síochána] permission to kick in the doors of someone’s dwelling in Ireland”.

“It’s unusual for the Irish state to be acting in such a clandestine manner,” Mulholland said. He has asked authorities to produce a search warrant and an itemized list of what was taken. “My fear is that whatever was taken has been put on a plane and taken to the US,” he added.

“This [extradition case] shows the complete disregard for due process … that the Trump administration seems to have,” Mulholland said.

articles.summary: Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
articles.preview: Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region. Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow. articles.body:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".

The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.

Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near MoÅodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.

He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.

A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa DÄba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.

Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".

In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".

European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.

The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.

This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.

Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.

Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.

The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.body: Smoke billowed over Kyiv and flames tore through apartment blocks and offices after Russia unleashed more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles across Ukraine overnight, killing at least eight people, six of them in the capital, and injuring 15, according to Ukrainian authorities and emergency services. Alongside residential and commercial buildings, strikes hit hospitals, essential infrastructure and three bridges spanning the Dnipro River, leaving streets littered with shattered masonry, twisted metal and wrecked cars. Across the battered capital, firefighters battled blazes while rescue teams searched ruined structures for survivors, police combed the debris for forensic evidence and utility crews worked to restore vital services. Some fires had been brought under control, but responders continued working to extinguish remaining blazes, clear rubble and assess damage across the capital. The devastating barrage, coming just a day after an earlier wave of attacks damaged diplomatic premises in Kyiv, made good on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s warning of a "painful" retaliation for Ukraine’s strike on the Crimean Bridge earlier in the week.

articles.body:
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.

Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.

Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied Crimean peninsula.

The latest Russian strikes coincided with talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.

The overnight attack against Ukraine was spread across several cities and regions, Zelensky said, with residential buildings and energy facilities also hit.

Air raid sirens lasted non-stop throughout the night and were ongoing into the morning.

Zelensky said over 110 missiles and more than 400 attack drones were launched by Russia, adding that "particularly insidious" tactics to launch the waves in 20 to 30-minute internals made it "more difficult to extinguish fires, clear debris, and restore services".

The three bridges targeted in Kyiv - the Podilsko-Voskresensky Bridge, the Darnytskyi Bridge and the Southern Bridge - were closed to traffic.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged people to "avoid travelling into the city by private car unless absolutely necessary", adding to the disruption around the capital following a first round of strikes against vital crossings earlier this week.

At least seven people were killed and 17 more were injured, Klitschko added, with unspecified civilian facilities also hit.

Ukraine's major operation to take out the road section of the Crimean Bridge earlier this week was a tactical and symbolic blow for Moscow.

Since illegally annexing Crimea in 2014, Moscow has housed troops and military equipment there, with occupying forces travelling through the peninsula towards the front line.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said an operation to weaken the bridge's defences and ultimately cause part of it to collapse had been weeks in the making.

Russian President Vladimir Putin - who personally opened the bridge in 2019 to international condemnation - said the Kremlin's retaliation for the strike would be "far more painful".

Of the nine fatalities confirmed so far, seven were in Kyiv and two were in Lviv, with at least 28 people injured.

The Sknyliv railway station in Lviv, a city in western Ukraine which has become one of the primary entry points to Ukraine for people and international aid, was badly damaged, the city's Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said.

The attack began hours after European leaders including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said they were ready for negotiations involving Moscow to end the war in Ukraine.

The Berlin meeting of the so-called coalition of the willing, an international alliance of Ukraine's allies committed to providing security support in the event of a peace deal, was attended by Zelensky and US President Donald Trump's envoys.

Jared Kushner said the US "wants to make a deal with Europe by his side" after fears of an agreement negotiated between the US and Russia were reignited by Trump's one-to-one talks with Putin earlier this week.

He claimed Russia was "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on Nato's Article Five, which requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

On Monday, Russia's deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov pushed back against that, saying "quasi-Nato" membership for Ukraine would be "unacceptable" to Russia. The Kremlin has long cited the prospect of Ukraine joining Nato as a key justification for its war effort.

The US president dialled into the Berlin talks from Air Force One on his way back from China, where he met his Russian counterpart and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

He reportedly questioned the decision of European leaders to commit â¬70bn (Â£58.6bn; $76.bn) in military funding for Ukraine.

The UK and France are jointly leading the first military exercise organised by the coalition of the willing, which involves thousands of troops from 11 countries and is taking place in Poland.

On Friday, Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Russia of an "intentional provocation" after a Russian cruise missile landed in his country.

It struck around 50km (31 miles) from its border with Ukraine, the Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Friday.

Two more unidentified projectiles, suspected to be a drone and a second missile, landed in villages nearby and no one was harmed, he added.

Polish and Swedish jets were scrambled on Nato's eastern flank as Russia's attack on western Ukraine continued. They have since been stood down.

France's foreign minister Jean-Noël Barro has called for a meeting of the UN Security Council following Russia's attack on Kyiv.

He described the strikes, which reportedly damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies, as "crimes" that "Russia will have to answer for".

articles.title: I politici in corteo a Roma, la cronaca di una giornata

Schlein: "Pessima manovra del governo" "Con le altre opposizioni abbiamo presentato 18 emendamenti unitari per mettere 4 miliardi in più per salvare la sanità pubblica che stanno smantellando, per rimettere in gioco il congedo paritario, per aiutare le famiglie, per approvare un salario minimo per riuscire finalmente a dare respiro all'economia di questo Paese e ai suoi lavoratori, quindi andremo avanti a mobilitarci insieme uniti contro questa manovra e parteciperemo anche alle prossime mobilitazioni di altre organizzazioni contro questa pessima manovra che per fortuna è l'ultima del governo Meloni", aggiunge Schlein. "Dobbiamo investire sulla scuola, sull'istruzione, sulla ricerca e sulla sanità. Dobbiamo restituire anche quel salasso operato a carico del ceto medio e dei pensionati. Dobbiamo voltare pagina e tirare fuori l'Italia da questa economia di guerra. Lo faremo tutti insieme", aggiunge il presidente M5s. "Voglio dire a Giorgia Meloni: dal Paese ti è arrivato un avviso di sfratto, andiamo a votare il più rapidamente possibile perché noi vogliamo cambiare le politiche economiche e sociali di questo Paese", aggiunge l'esponente Avs. Bonelli rivolge poi un messaggio ai giovani in corteo: "Agli studenti dico, fate bene a battervi, scendete in piazza e non date retta a questa destra o a questi signori perbenisti che vi vorrebbero chiusi dentro casa. Fratoianni: “L'emergenza italiana sono gli stipendi” "Questa manifestazione è molto grande, come lo sono quelle che in questo momento stanno riempiendo le strade di tutta Italia. Oggi è lo sciopero generale: lavoratori, lavoratrici, studenti, cittadini in piazza per chiedere giustizia e diritti, dire no all'aumento della spesa militare e chiedere risorse per sanità, istruzione, ricerca e per alzare gli stipendi", afferma Nicola Fratoianni a margine del corteo Cgil a Roma. "L'emergenza italiana si chiama stipendi, fermi al palo mentre il costo della vita cresce senza sosta. Così questo Paese si schianta e non ce la fa più e la manovra di Meloni non risponde a nessuno di questi bisogni, va in direzione ostinata e contraria, oltre che sbagliata. Noi lavoreremo per cambiarla: se non la cambiano loro, cambieremo noi queste politiche quando li batteremo nelle urne". "È l'ora che lascino Palazzo Chigi, hanno fallito e questo Paese lo grida ogni giorno", aggiunge l'esponente Avs che sottolinea ancora: "Oggi manifesta l'Italia che chiede un cambiamento, che rivendica futuro e che non si accontenta di un presente fatto di precarietà, diritto allo studio negato e diritti universali, come quello alla salute, negati. Noi stiamo con questa Italia".

articles.title: Ukraine: Kyiv metro stations become overnight shelters amid air raids
articles.summary: Residents of Kyiv, Ukraine, sought refuge in underground metro stations overnight on Thursday 19 November 2026, as repeated air raid alerts warned of further Russian attacks on the capital. Strikes on the Ukrainian capital killed at least one person, injured five and damaged two embassies.
articles.preview: Residents of Kyiv, Ukraine, sought refuge in underground metro stations overnight on Thursday 19 November 2026, as repeated air raid alerts warned of further Russian attacks on the capital. Strikes on the Ukrainian capital killed at least one person, injured five and damaged two embassies.
articles.body: Carrying bags and personal belongings, Kyiv residents filed down into the capital’s metro stations to spend the night underground, pitching makeshift tents and laying out inflatable mattresses along the platforms as air-raid sirens warned of incoming missiles and drones. Above ground, a large-scale Russian assault killed at least three people and injured at least 15, according to updated tolls from Mayor Vitali Klitschko, while damaging residential buildings, a landmark cathedral, bridges across the Dnipro River and the Austrian, Dutch and Brazilian embassies. All diplomatic staff escaped without injury, though an explosion blew out windows and damaged cars at the Austrian embassy while staff were inside, and a nearby projectile impact caused light damage to the Dutch mission. The barrage came shortly after Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed that Moscow would answer Ukraine’s strikes on the Crimean Bridge with retaliation that would be “much more painful”. Throughout the conflict, Kyiv’s metro network has served as an indispensable subterranean sanctuary, offering protection to civilians whenever Russian attacks put homes, offices and urban infrastructure in the crosshairs.

articles.title: One in four children lived in conflict zones in 2025, Save the Children warns
articles.summary: Save the Children warns that the situation could deteriorate further in 2026, as fighting continues across the Middle East, including Iran, Lebanon and Yemen.
articles.preview: Protection of children Nearly 589 million children – one in four worldwide – lived in conflict zones in 2025, the highest number recorded since the end of the Cold War in 1990, according to an annual report by Save the Children. The vast majority are in the Middle East and Africa, where prolonged conflicts continue to expose children to hunger, displacement, injury and psychological trauma.
articles.body:
Protection of children

Nearly 589 million children – one in four worldwide – lived in conflict zones in 2025, the highest number recorded since the end of the Cold War in 1990, according to an annual report by Save the Children.

The vast majority are in the Middle East and Africa, where prolonged conflicts continue to expose children to hunger, displacement, injury and psychological trauma.

In Yemen, a young girl diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition is fighting for her life, while a six-year-old boy is still recovering after an unexploded device detonated as he walked home from school, leaving him with serious injuries and lasting trauma.

In Syria, years of conflict have forced children from their homes repeatedly. Many now live in overcrowded displacement camps or makeshift shelters, with limited access to education and basic services.

Save the Children warns that the situation could deteriorate further in 2026, as fighting continues across the Middle East, including Iran, Lebanon and Yemen.

Despite a ceasefire, conditions in Gaza also remain dire, with continued strikes and restricted access to essential supplies.

The organisation says millions of children remain trapped in conflict, facing threats to their lives, education and future.

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin release 'peace declaration' from unprecedented summit
articles.summary: The leaders "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and pledged to advance United Nations reforms, increase supplies of fuel products for all countries, and uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.
articles.preview: The leaders "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and pledged to advance United Nations reforms, increase supplies of fuel products for all countries, and uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts. BEIJING: China, the United States and Russia agreed on a symbolic "peace declaration" at an unprecedented three-way summit on Thursday (Nov 19) and reaffirmed that nuclear war should never be fought, but announced no plans for arms control talks long sought by Trump.
articles.body:
The leaders "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and pledged to advance United Nations reforms, increase supplies of fuel products for all countries, and uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.

BEIJING: China, the United States and Russia agreed on a symbolic "peace declaration" at an unprecedented three-way summit on Thursday (Nov 19) and reaffirmed that nuclear war should never be fought, but announced no plans for arms control talks long sought by Trump.

A joint declaration released by Chinese President Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin capped a three-day diplomatic swing by Trump through Asia that produced few tangible victories, despite his repeated boasts about making history and brokering peace.

Instead, the trip raised fresh questions among US allies about his increasingly close relationships with Xi and with Putin, who continues to wage war against Ukraine.

Trump greeted Putin as "my friend" and received a hug from Xi in the latest of the diplomatic spectacles he favours.

Those meetings, which have included discussions with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and summits with Putin, have drawn praise from some for his willingness to engage directly with US adversaries and criticism from others for giving autocrats a global stage.

The leaders pledged to advance United Nations reforms, increase supplies of fuel products for all countries, and uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.

The declaration did not mention Russia's war in Ukraine or the US conflict with Iran, and in a press conference afterwards, Putin acknowledged it did not set ambitious goals and added that nobody would be forced to comply with its decisions.

The powers "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and added that they would "conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation of nuclear weapons", without giving a time frame.

But the statement made no mention of negotiations on a trilateral nuclear arms reduction treaty, something Trump has pushed since his first term and that China has consistently rejected, arguing that its arsenal is much smaller than those of the other powers.

Trump referred to nuclear weapons at the start of the meeting, saying: "It’s not an easy thing to do - give them up."

He told NBC afterwards that it "went great".

"On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12," he said. "Fantastic relationships built."

In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said he would hold a news conference in Washington at noon on Friday.

China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi said the countries would maintain coordination at working level after the "peace summit".

Analysts said Trump came to Shenzhen seeking to bolster his standing after his Republican Party lost control of Congress in midterm elections this month.

Trump told Reuters the Shenzhen summit was "bigger than Yalta", referring to the 1945 conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union, which became shorthand for great-power deals.

He defended calling Putin a friend, saying that "it's nice to have people that have 4,000 nuclear weapons as a friend as opposed to an enemy".

He also called Xi a friend and "an amazing leader", but acknowledged the difficulty of achieving nuclear-arms cuts, saying it was "psychologically very difficult" for leaders.

Charles Schumer, who leads Democrats in the US Senate, called the trilateral summit "a historic embarrassment that people will remember long into the future".

"It's a betrayal of the United States by a president who loves nothing more than to bow down to our adversaries for a photo op," he said.

Daryl Kimball, executive director of the US-based Arms Control Association, called the reaffirmation that a nuclear war should not be fought "positive, but said, "We need much more than rhetoric. We need action on disarmament diplomacy".

The reference to immunity of state officials came more than three years after the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and other Russian officials over alleged war crimes in Ukraine. Moscow rejects the allegations.

"The pushback against international norms and courts is the most interesting aspect," said Jonathan Eyal, international director at the Royal United Services Institute think-tank in London. "The big powers dictate, the small powers suffer."

Eyal said Putin had been a winner from the summit and "gained credibility and escape from pariah status", while Trump "gained a photo opportunity he didn't need".

International relations analyst Minran Liu said the trilateral helped reinforce Russia's standing as a major power alongside the US and China.

“Putin, simply by being present at this meeting, can consolidate his domestic power … (putting) Russia on equal footing with the US and China. Russia's economy is one-tenth of China’s, so this is a big win for Russia,” the University of Queensland lecturer told CNA’s Asia First.

James Crabtree, a distinguished visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, said the meeting carried significant implications for Washington's relationships with its traditional allies.

“It really underlines the unreliability of the US for its traditional allies and partners – Japan, South Korea, Australia, the Europeans, the countries that used to see the US as the bedrock of the international system. But it doesn't play that role under Trump,” he told CNA’s Asia Tonight.

VILLA BY A LAKE

The leaders met in a villa in wooded hills beside a lake in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.

"We are really making history," Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. "No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement."

Xi in his turn said: "History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace. When major powers clash, the world falls into turmoil."

European allies met in Berlin on Thursday to back Ukraine and warned against deciding peace terms over their heads.

"A 'Yalta' format will not bring peace," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters, adding that leaders would not allow Europe to be divided up. He sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as "a photo opportunity".

"The US understands that there can be no peace without us," he said.

Standing alongside Merz, Trump's son-in-law and special envoy Jared Kushner stressed that Trump wanted a peace deal with Europe at his side and that Russia had agreed to engage in multilateral talks with Europe. He said Trump had dialled into the Berlin summit and came away from his meeting with Putin and Xi believing "peace is achievable".

The US and Europe, close allies for decades after the end of World War Two, have moved apart as Trump has scaled back support for Ukraine and insisted NATO partners pay more for their own defence.

Asked by a reporter about Trump greeting Putin as "my friend" in Shenzhen, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy simply shrugged and walked on.

The trilateral meeting was a diplomatic coup for Putin, with Russia’s economy barely a tenth the size of China's and most of its businesses barred from trading with the West by sanctions.

Putin said the three countries had "numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine".

He rejected criticism comparing the summit to Yalta, saying that summit had not divided the world into spheres of influence but "codified the existing reality".

Underlying diplomatic tensions could resurface in a few weeks when Trump hosts the Group of 20 summit at his golf resort in Florida, where he is expected to meet Xi again and potentially Putin.

Putin, whose presence would likely anger the US allies, said he would consider attending, having discussed it with Trump, but would need to take the situation in Russia into account.

articles.title: Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?
articles.summary: Russian President Putin has suggested evacuating civilians from the embattled Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka. But experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?
