articles.body:
November 19, 2026

Russian President Putin has suggested evacuating civilians from the embattled Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka. But experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

What is the situation for civilians?

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.

Humanitarian proposals as leverage

Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.

Ceasefire as military tactic

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

How should Kyiv respond to Moscow's proposal?

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Dl scuola, gli e-book spaccano la maggioranza. FI vota contro, poi l'emendamento passa in Senato
articles.summary: AGI - L'avvertimento era arrivato ieri: Forza Italia è contraria alla norma sugli e-book . Ma FdI ha tenuto il punto sull'emendamento che stabilisce per gli editori l'obbligo di vendere la versione digitale dei libri scolastici e universitari a un prezzo inferiore di almeno il 50% rispetto alle edizioni cartacee. E così la maggioranza al Senato si spacca, con gli azzurri che votano contro e Azione che si aggiunge ai voti favorevoli delle altre forze di centrodestra. L'emendamento passa in Aula L'emendamento, presentato al Decreto Scuola, che tra le altre norme introduce il tetto del 30% di alunni stranieri con insufficiente conoscenza dell'italiano nelle classi, viene prima bocciato in Commissione Bilancio, sempre con i voti contrari di Forza Italia. Poi, messo in votazione in Aula, passa per 8 voti di differenza (84 sì e 76 no), con il via libera di FdI, presenti in massa, Lega e Noi Moderati, a cui si aggiungono i voti dei calendiani. Contrarie tutte le altre forze di opposizione, che protestano in Aula con cartelli e slogan. Il decreto, alla fine, viene approvato con i sì di tutto il centrodestra (80 voti favorevoli e 46 contrari) e trasmesso alla Camera per il via libera definitivo. articles.title: Meloni: "Non può esserci pace in Ucraina senza l'Europa"
articles.summary: AGI - "A Dublino, noi leader abbiamo stabilito come accompagnare questo processo: un team europeo", nel cosiddetto formato E5, nel quale è presente l'Italia, "che lavora in stretta collaborazione con l'Ucraina e gli Stati Uniti. Ora dobbiamo conferire a questo team un mandato chiaro: cosa chiediamo, cosa offriamo e cosa non accetteremo mai". Così la presidente del Consiglio, Giorgia Meloni, si è rivolta ai partecipanti al vertice dei Volenterosi per l'Ucraina a Berlino. "E non ci presentiamo a mani vuote", ha sottolineato ancora la premier, "questa coalizione sta lavorando a garanzie di sicurezza, incluso l'impegno ispirato all'Articolo 5 proposto dall'Italia - un modello che ora si trova sul tavolo negoziale". Meloni: "Non può esserci pace senza l'Europa" "Oggi - ha continuato Meloni - i leader di Stati Uniti, Russia e Cina si sono incontrati a Shenzhen. La loro dichiarazione parla di stabilità strategica, energia e rischi nucleari. Accogliamo con favore l'impegno a evitare che una guerra nucleare venga mai combattuta. Tuttavia, nel testo non si fa menzione della guerra in Ucraina. Ciò ci suggerisce due cose. Primo: la Cina conta in questo conflitto e, se intende essere una forza di stabilità, questo è il momento di esercitare la propria influenza per spingere la Russia verso una pace reale. Secondo: è chiaro a tutti che non può esserci pace in Ucraina senza l'Ucraina. E non può esserci pace senza l'Europa". La pressione sulla Russia e gli attacchi alle infrastrutture energetiche Meloni ha poi osservato: "Quanto ai russi, francamente, non so cosa aspettarmi. Lo scambio di prigionieri concordato ad Abu Dhabi è un segnale positivo; accogliamo con favore ogni passo di natura umanitaria. Ma la vera prova consiste nell'interruzione verificabile degli attacchi alle infrastrutture energetiche". "A Shenzhen, i tre leader hanno ribadito l'importanza di flussi energetici stabili. Bene. Prendiamoli in parola, a cominciare dalla rete elettrica ucraina. È una questione che ci riguarda tutti: la sicurezza delle centrali nucleari nel nostro continente, milioni di civili che affrontano l'inverno, mercati energetici già sotto pressione. Se Mosca dovesse opporsi, il mondo vedrà chiaramente chi desidera la pace e chi no. Nel frattempo, continuiamo a sostenere l'Ucraina e a mantenere alta la pressione sulla Russia". "L'Italia - ha concluso Meloni - sta facendo la sua parte e continuerà a farla: abbiamo appena adottato un nuovo pacchetto di aiuti militari, proseguiremo il lavoro sulle garanzie, contribuiremo al team negoziale europeo e sosterremo la ricostruzione dell'Ucraina - un impegno che portiamo avanti sin dalla Conferenza sulla ricostruzione tenutasi a Roma". Gli Stati Uniti vogliono accelerare il percorso verso la pace Fonti italiane hanno poi riferito che "gli Stati Uniti hanno ribadito la volontà di arrivare il prima possibile a una pace in Ucraina", sottolineando che "è emersa una volontà da parte di tutti di cogliere un momentum che si crede, si pensa essere particolarmente favorevole", con Washington intenzionata a imprimere un'accelerazione al percorso verso una soluzione del conflitto e gli europei chiamati a dare concretezza al proprio contributo. Non soltanto sul piano economico, ma anche attraverso un'agenda politica e negoziale definita, sulla quale si continuerà a lavorare a livello di consiglieri, insieme agli inviati speciali americani e ucraini. Il siparietto con Merz e il colloquio con Kushner Meloni ha lasciato il summit al termine dei lavori per volare a Roma e collegarsi con gli altri leader di centrodestra per fare il punto sulla manovra. Al suo arrivo in Cancelleria, dove si è svolto il summit, la premier è stata protagonista di un simpatico siparietto: l'auto su cui viaggiava non si è fermata davanti al tappeto rosso allestito dal cerimoniale, ma solo qualche metro più avanti, e ha dovuto fare una breve retromarcia. "Giorgia, vai troppo veloce", ha scherzato Merz prima di abbracciarla e stringerle la mano. A margine della foto di famiglia, la premier ha avuto anche un breve colloquio con Jared Kushner, uno dei due inviati Usa per l'Ucraina, nonché genero di Trump.

articles.title: Nearly a quarter of the world’s children live in conflict zones, according to Save the Children
articles.summary: A 'record rate' of 589 million children were living in war zones in 2025, with 44% of them in Africa.
articles.preview: Nearly a quarter of the world's children are currently living in a conflict zone, a record rate since statistics were first recorded in the 1990s, the charity Save the Children said on Thursday, November 19. "Almost one in four children worldwide are now living in conflict zones, the highest number since records began in 1990," the London-based charity said. "The figure represents an increase of more than 50% in a decade, jumping from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025," it added.
articles.body:
Nearly a quarter of the world's children are currently living in a conflict zone, a record rate since statistics were first recorded in the 1990s, the charity Save the Children said on Thursday, November 19.

"Almost one in four children worldwide are now living in conflict zones, the highest number since records began in 1990," the London-based charity said. "The figure represents an increase of more than 50% in a decade, jumping from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025," it added.

The report was titled "Stop the War on Children: Changing the Odds" and drew on statistics from the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO). The percentage of children living in conflict zones has doubled from 10% in the mid-1990s to 23.4% in 2025.

"These record-high figures are a stark reminder that conflict is devastating the daily lives, education, health and future prospects of hundreds of millions of children," said Gudrun Ostby, a research professor at PRIO. "Unless greater efforts are made to protect children in conflict settings, the consequences of today's wars will be felt for decades to come," he added.

The report defines conflict zones as areas existing within a 50-kilometer radius in which at least one armed attack took place. Africa has the largest number of children living in conflict zones, at about 260 million, or 44% of the total across the globe, the report found.

Rates have surged in the Middle East as well, from 52 million children in 2024 to 67 million in 2025, a 29% increase. An average of two in five children in Africa and the Middle East are living in conflict zones, it added.

"The scale of this crisis is rapidly growing, and the systems meant to protect children are being pushed to breaking point," said Inger Ashing, chief executive of Save The Children International.

articles.title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
articles.summary: A mathematician at Anthropic says he used an AI to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis, though verification will take some time.
articles.preview: An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis. Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem. If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
articles.body:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."

"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

The complete proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 lines long.

Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.

No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

Attackers are using increasingly sophisticated methods as AI advances, and unauthorized access has led to a string of personal data leaks in Japan. The increase in claims raises the risk of costly payouts even as rising numbers of incidents fuel demand for protection.

Payouts on cyber policies could rise, but the surge has yet to translate into a significant earnings hit. Yoshinari Endo, a managing executive officer at Tokio Marine, said his company expects some impact on full-year results, though it is managing the profit risk and expects losses to stay within the assumptions of its initial annual plan.

Junsuke Koike, an executive vice president at Sompo, said inquiries about raising coverage amounts or adding coverage items had tripled from normal levels.

Japan’s experience mirrors a broader rise in cyber claims globally. US insurers reported more than 56,000 cyber claims in 2025, up 20% from a year earlier, while large companies are facing increasingly costly incidents. Cyber policies typically cover damages owed for data breaches, recovery costs and profits lost from disruptions, making insurance a growing part of corporate risk management.

Cyber insurance penetration in Japan remains low for smaller companies. A 2025 survey by the General Insurance Association of Japan found that only 8.8% of small and medium-sized business owners said they had cyber insurance as a defense against attacks.

Yasuko Fukuda, a senior executive officer at MS&AD Insurance Group Holdings, said at an earnings briefing on Thursday that there is “significant room for the market to expand.”

The insurers are trying to limit losses by helping customers prevent attacks. Starting in December, Sompo will offer a new service with Trend Micro and others that monitors for vulnerabilities on the internet.

Insurers are being selective about underwriting. Tokio Marine may cap payouts or tighten coverage terms depending on a customer’s risk profile, Endo said. The company expects its cyber insurance business to remain profitable in the fiscal year through March 2027. Standard total payout limits in Japan and overseas run from about ¥100 million (about $630,000) to several hundred million yen per contract.

articles.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
articles.summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
articles.preview: Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down. The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors. Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
articles.body:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.

But tech stocks more broadly also fell.

Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

articles.body:
Wall Street chiude in forte calo. Dj cede il 2,03% a 48.102,46 punti, il Nasdaq cede il 5,37% a 22.596,71 punti e lo S500 lascia il 3,81% a 6.902,25 punti.

La quotazione da record di Anthropic non basta ai mercati. Il successo dello sbarco a Wall Street non spazza via i timori sulla sostenibilità del settore e, anzi, li accentua. Dall'Asia all'Europa passando per gli Stati Uniti, tutte le piazze finanziarie sono in profondo rosso con gli investitori preoccupati su quanto potrà durare il boom dell'IA. Tokyo e Seul hanno chiuso rispettivamente in calo del 5,26% e del 5,21%.

L'Europa ha archiviato al seduta in profondo rosso bruciando 370 miliardi di capitalizzazione. Francoforte è scesa del 2,60% e Milano del 2,48% appesantita dai significativi cali di Stm (-10,78%), Technoprobe (-9,31%) e Prysmian (-6,29%), che risentono dei timori dello scoppio della bolla sull'intelligenza artificiale.

Gli analisti danno per scontato un ritocco al rialzo di un quarto di punto a dicembre, e non escludono una nuova stretta a gennaio a fronte della galoppata dell'inflazione. "I tassi di interesse restano troppo alti a causa di una Fed politicizzata, e non sto pensando al presidente" della banca centrale, ha lamentato Donald Trump insistendo sul fatto che gli Stati Uniti dovrebbero avere i tassi più bassi del mondo.

Anthropic cale di oltre l'11% ma si mantiene sopra gli 83 dollari fissati nell'initial public offering. La sua quotazione è stata accompagnata da due sedute di vendite sui listini americani, appesantiti dai timori sulla capacità della startup di mantenere i suoi livelli di capitalizzazione e da come il settore potrebbe essere regolato. "Chi vince nell'IA, vince. Mi batterò per i data center", ha detto Trump annunciando un inasprimento delle tasse per le aziende che decideranno di costruire data center fuori dagli Stati Uniti.

"Non possono farlo, li prenderebbe la Cina", ha spiegato prima di lodare la quotazione di Anthropic. "E' stata un successo, ho un grande rispetto per Dario" Amodei, l'amministratore delegato, ha aggiunto Trump facendo eco alle parole del suo segretario di Tesoro, che ha descritto l'initial public offering della startp una "storia tutta americana".

Ma non è solo la nuova entrata a Wall Street a tremare: in forte calo è l'intero settore tecnologico, da settimane sotto pressione per lo scandalo Nvidia. Il colosso dei semiconduttori perde oltre il 7% nonostante la trimestrale sopra le attese dei giorni scorsi e l'impegno dei nuovi vertici ad aumentare i salari dei dipendenti nel tentativo di risollevare il loro morale. Le indiscrezioni che si susseguono su Nvidia e il suo ex amministratore delegato però penalizzano i titoli. Il New York Times ha riportato che in aprile il gigante dei chip ha chiesto alle autorità americane l'autorizzazione a vendere più di 40.000 chip H20 a una società legata a Megaspeed e Alice Huang, la donna che l'intelligence statunitense ritiene una spia cinese.

Secondo il quotidiano, inoltre, Huang non era amato da tutti all'interno della società per il suo stile "minaccioso, offensivo e minatorio" nei confronti del personale. Un ex vicepresidente delle risorse umane di Nvidia, Michael Winston, è stato licenziato nel 2005 per aver sollevato perplessità sulla condotta di Huang, riporta il New York Times. "Pensa di poterla fare franca in qualsiasi cosa", aveva detto Winston sul suo ex capo.

Con Nvidia sono in calo anche i titoli degli altri colossi dei semiconduttori, a partire da Advanced Micro Devices che cede più dell'11% dopo che la società di investimento Hunterbrook Media ha denunciato che Amd ha continuano a fornire alla cinese IEIT i suoi chip nonostante fosse sulla lista nera delle autorità americane.

articles.title: Il ceo di Anthropic in Puglia, riserbo sui motivi della visita
articles.summary: L'arrivo a Brindisi. Forse in vacanza in un resort, c'è chi sostiene sia alla ricerca di una masseria
articles.preview: In Puglia tutti cercano Dario Amodei, l'amministratore delegato e cofondatore di Anthropic, colosso dell'intelligenza artificiale, che stamattina, a sorpresa, è atterrato all'aeroporto di Brindisi con il suo jet privato. T-shirt bianca a maniche corte, pantalone nero, sneakers e tracolla in pelle, è uscito attorno a mezzogiorno dallo scalo brindisino assieme ad alcuni amici e circondato dai suoi bodyguard.
articles.body:
In Puglia tutti cercano Dario Amodei, l'amministratore delegato e cofondatore di Anthropic, colosso dell'intelligenza artificiale, che stamattina, a sorpresa, è atterrato all'aeroporto di Brindisi con il suo jet privato.

T-shirt bianca a maniche corte, pantalone nero, sneakers e tracolla in pelle, è uscito attorno a mezzogiorno dallo scalo brindisino assieme ad alcuni amici e circondato dai suoi bodyguard. Le immagini del suo arrivo sono state diffuse dall'emittente televisiva pugliese Antenna Sud: lo ritraggono mentre stringe ancora tra le mani il cuscino da viaggio gonfiabile per il collo, a testimonianza del lungo viaggio fatto, e mentre raggiunge la Range Rover sulla quale si allontanerà con le numerose valigia al seguito.

Massimo riserbo su quelli che potrebbero essere gli impegni dell'imprenditore italo-americano in queste ore in Puglia. Tra le ipotesi, anche una vacanza di circa una settimana in uno dei lussuosi resort a poca distanza dal mare e immerso negli ulivi secolari del Brindisino. I sospetti sono tutti concentrati su Borgo Egnazia, dove la premier Giorgia Meloni organizzò nel giugno del 2024 il G7. Ma dal resort 5 stelle lusso smentiscono: "Abbiamo effettuato le verifiche necessarie e ci dispiace informarla che nessuno dei nostri ospiti corrisponde al nome da lei indicato", rispondono con la solita cortesia.

Ma non è escluso che la prenotazione sia stata fatta con un altro nome, come accade di solito. Quello che sembra essere certo è che a Borgo Egnazia oggi era in programma una riunione molto riservata tra esperti che parlavano di Intelligenza artificiale e del suo sviluppo tecnologico. Ma anche su questo le bocche sono cucite.

Non si esclude che Amodei e gli amici possano proseguire la loro vacanza a bordo di uno yacht privato già arrivato a Brindisi. Inutile chiedere notizie a Polizia, Carabinieri, Guardia Costiera, sindaci e politici del territorio. Nessuno dice di sapere dove si trovi il ceo di Anthropic che, secondo altre fonti, potrebbe essere atterrato in Salento anche per valutare l'acquisto di una masseria.

Il suo arrivo in Puglia segue di poche ore il debutto di Anthropic a Wall Street, dove ieri è stata quotata con il simbolo Ant con una raccolta record, superiore a quella di SpaceX. Oggi, però, il titolo perde il 10% mantenendosi comunque sopra gli 83 dollari per azione, il prezzo fissato nell'Initial public offering.

articles.title: Daniel Ek backs AI researcher’s fusion power startup. Here’s what they’re building.
articles.summary: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher. Here's what the startup is building.
articles.preview: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant. The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.
articles.body:
Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”

articles.title: Super-hot rock geothermal could end data center energy woes
articles.summary: New geothermal startups are betting that they can leapfrog today's leaders to deliver terawatts of electricity nearly anywhere.
articles.preview: Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all. The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal. Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration.
articles.body:
Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all.

The broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal.

Geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers.

An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential.

The secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more.

Super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy said on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep.

Google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the company’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo.

Meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy announced it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop and refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists.

XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches.

Quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the company will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures.

Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool.

The startup’s newly announced technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused.

In both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive.

Investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors, including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors, including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates.

As with any new technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO2-cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch.

That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up.

articles.title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
articles.summary: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics's most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world's best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval
articles.preview: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics's most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world's best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval
articles.body:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.

An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.

Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.

The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.

A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:

I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.

The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”

Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”

In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.

OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.

OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.

Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

articles.title: Behind Jensen Huang’s exit, questions about a management style reportedly built on fear
articles.summary: Elon Musk may have been overstating it when he said Nvidia’s employees “love” the ousted Jensen Huang.
articles.preview: Earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he said, “They love [Huang]. They love him.” Well, maybe not all of them.
articles.body:
Earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he said, “They love [Huang]. They love him.”

Well, maybe not all of them. Thousands of employees have signed a letter asking for Huang’s return, but others tell The New York Times he ruled through praise and fear, as well as by humiliating people.

According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate employees with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.

Naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been said, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications.

articles.title: US: Protesters demand human control over AI after Anthropic's IPO
articles.summary: Protesters gathered outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters on 19 November 2026 to demand tighter regulation and greater human control over artificial intelligence, following the company’s $2 trillion stock market debut.

Apple is developing its own autonomous artificial intelligence agent that can get things done on behalf of users, looking to enter a fast-growing market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta Platforms and others.

The company outlined the plans in job listings added to its website this week. In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

The move follows the breakout success of Meta’s Muse, which has captured the attention of consumers in recent months with its ability to make restaurant reservations, book travel and prepare news briefings. There’s also been a proliferation of tools that let AI control Mac computers and program software.

articles.summary: Journalists were told the move was a cybersecurity precaution against potential espionage attempts.
articles.preview: The White House took phones away from reporters traveling with U.S. President Donald Trump upon his departure from China, an unusual move. Trump departed Shenzhen on Thursday following meetings with the Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. articles.body:
The White House took phones away from reporters traveling with U.S. President Donald Trump upon his departure from China, an unusual move.

Trump departed Shenzhen on Thursday following meetings with the Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.

The press pool’s phones were taken “for security reasons,” according to a pool report on departure. Further information was not immediately provided.

A subsequent pool report, issued after Air Force One landed in the U.S. some 15 hours later, said a staff member had collected a number of mobile phones from reporters when they boarded the presidential plane, placing them in a bag designed to block signals. Journalists were told the move was a cybersecurity precaution against potential espionage attempts.

Reporters were given their telephones back after landing in the United States.

Protocols are sometimes shifted for security reasons, but the precise reason for this time was unclear. The Air Force One aircraft Trump was traveling aboard on the flight home from Shenzhen is a Qatari-gifted, Boeing luxury jumbo jet that is serving as a temporary presidential aircraft. The newer plane flew directly back to a military base near Washington, avoiding a refueling stop in Alaska that is customary for Air Force One flights between the U.S. and Asia.

Security protocols around the president’s travel have come under increased scrutiny since July, when Trump covertly switched planes in Turkey before a flight to the U.K., an elaborate ruse that was eventually revealed to have been prompted by an Iranian assassination threat. The president later said the maneuver came at the request of the military and the Secret Service.

articles.title: La Anthropic in borsa tra miliardi e promesse
articles.summary: L’azienda ha raccolto 81 miliardi di dollari. I fondatori ne hanno blindato il controllo, con un accentramento del potere che fa sorgere molti dubbi
articles.preview: Il 19 novembre 2026 l’azienda d’intelligenza artificiale (ia) Anthropic ha fatto il suo debutto alla borsa statunitense, anticipando quello della rivale OpenAi, che pure era stata la prima protagonista del settore grazie al lancio di ChatGpt quattro anni fa. I numeri sono da capogiro: la Anthropic, artefice del chatbot Claude, ha venduto 980 milioni di azioni a 83 dollari l’una, cioè una quantità più alta del previsto (la stima era di 825 milioni) a un prezzo più alto di quello che tutti si aspettavano a Wall street (70-78 dollari).
articles.body:
Il 19 novembre 2026 l’azienda d’intelligenza artificiale (ia) Anthropic ha fatto il suo debutto alla borsa statunitense, anticipando quello della rivale OpenAi, che pure era stata la prima protagonista del settore grazie al lancio di ChatGpt quattro anni fa.

I numeri sono da capogiro: la Anthropic, artefice del chatbot Claude, ha venduto 980 milioni di azioni a 83 dollari l’una, cioè una quantità più alta del previsto (la stima era di 825 milioni) a un prezzo più alto di quello che tutti si aspettavano a Wall street (70-78 dollari).

L’operazione ha fruttato 81 miliardi di dollari, dando vita al più ricco collocamento in borsa di sempre e attestando il valore dell’Anthropic sui 1.500 miliardi. Altri 26 miliardi potrebbero arrivare da un gruppo di grandi investitori, tra cui la Nvidia e Google, attraverso una vendita privata. Un risultato ancora più impressionante se si pensa che l’Anthropic è nata sei anni fa.

La buona riuscita del collocamento in un certo senso interrompe i giorni cupi vissuti dal settore dell’ia in seguito alla scandalo della Nvidia e alle dimissioni del suo amministratore delegato Jensen Huang. E offre una pausa al timore diffuso che stia per scoppiare un’enorme bolla finanziaria. La stessa Anthropic aveva ridimensionato le previsioni sul debutto in borsa, stimando di poter raggiungere un valore di duemila miliardi di dollari.

Invece gli investitori che hanno cercato di accaparrarsi il titolo della Anthropic sono stati moltissimi, al punto da lamentarsi perché le azioni disponibili erano troppo poche.

Un potere illimitato

Alla fine del 19 novembre l’Anthropic si è ritrovata con un “tesoretto” di circa 94 miliardi di dollari. Soldi ovviamente destinati ad arricchire gli azionisti, ma non solo: in buona parte – si parla di 71 miliardi – saranno investiti nei data center e in generale nello sviluppo di nuove tecnologie nel 2027. Ed entro il 2045 l’azienda conta di investire novecento miliardi.

Tuttavia, il lancio della Anthropic sulla più grande piazza finanziaria del mondo è anche una grande sfida per dimostrare la sua effettiva solidità e in generale la capacità del settore dell’ia di affermarsi superando tutti i dubbi che lo circondano, innanzitutto quelli sulla possibilità di continuare a costruire data center in giro per il mondo e realizzare attività redditizie e davvero utili alle persone.

Fin dalla sua fondazione l’Anthropic ha sempre registrato perdite, anche se nei primi nove mesi del 2026 il suo fatturato è cresciuto del 1.200 per cento, arrivando a 33 miliardi di dollari. Ma ciò che più colpisce del suo collocamento è una decisione presa alla vigilia del suo ingresso del mondo del profitto a tutti i costi.

Lo spiega il settimanale tedesco Die Zeit: “L’azienda sostiene di essersi data un particolare meccanismo di tutela: una forma di separazione dei poteri per frenare la ricerca del profitto. In modo che l’ia della Anthropic continui a svilupparsi ‘a lungo termine a beneficio dell’umanità’”. Sarebbe un fatto senza precedenti, in effetti.

Nel prospetto della quotazione l’amministratore delegato Dario Amodei e gli altri sei fondatori dell’Anthropic hanno scritto che la loro ia potrebbe portare nel mondo sia cose positive sia cose negative: l’eradicazione di alcune malattie e una crescita economica senza precedenti; ma anche la creazione di sistemi di sorveglianza repressivi o consigli utili ai terroristi per la produzione di armi biologiche.

Per questo sentono la responsabilità di “aiutare il mondo a comprendere questi rischi e a prevenirli o mitigarli, qualora dovessero emergere dai nostri modelli d’ia”.

Sarà anche per questo che Amodei e i suoi soci hanno tenuto per sé una speciale categoria di azioni, denominata di classe F, che in teoria gli permetterà di controllare l’azienda all’infinito. O almeno di non farla cadere nelle mani di investitori e fondi speculativi che portano avanti piani altamente redditizi ma potenzialmente dannosi.

Una sorta di versione “istituzionalizzata” del famoso motto don’t be evil che aveva Google, osserva la Zeit. Ma questo presuppone che il potere illimitato di Amodei e soci sarà usato sempre nel modo giusto, senza scaricare il peso di eventuali danni sul resto della società.

Si può pure credere nella loro buona fede, ma le vicende recenti di Jensen Huang, un manager della Silicon valley dai poteri quasi illimitati, non dovrebbero far dormire sonni tranquilli a nessuno. ◆

articles.title: Quella di Anthropic è già la quotazione più grande di sempre
articles.summary: La società che sviluppa il chatbot Claude ha fissato il valore delle sue azioni a 83 dollari ciascuna
articles.preview: La società che sviluppa il chatbot Claude ha fissato il valore delle sue azioni a 83 dollari ciascuna Aggiornamento: nel frattempo Anthropic si è quotata in borsa, e il Post segue qui la quotazione Anthropic, la società di intelligenza artificiale (AI) che ha sviluppato il chatbot Claude, ha fissato a 83 dollari il prezzo delle azioni per la quotazione in borsa a New York di giovedì pomeriggio (ora italiana).
articles.body:
La società che sviluppa il chatbot Claude ha fissato il valore delle sue azioni a 83 dollari ciascuna

Aggiornamento: nel frattempo Anthropic si è quotata in borsa, e il Post segue qui la quotazione

Anthropic, la società di intelligenza artificiale (AI) che ha sviluppato il chatbot Claude, ha fissato a 83 dollari il prezzo delle azioni per la quotazione in borsa a New York di giovedì pomeriggio (ora italiana). Si tratta già in questa prima fase della più grande IPO (offerta pubblica iniziale di azioni) della storia: 83 dollari è il prezzo a cui sono state vendute in via preferenziale 980 milioni di azioni agli investitori – in questa fase perlopiù banche, fondi di investimento, e via così – e l’offerta è arrivata a un valore complessivo di 81,3 miliardi di dollari, attribuendo così all’intera società una valutazione di circa 1.500 miliardi di dollari.

Chi ha comprato queste azioni potrà rivenderle in borsa da oggi, quando all’apertura della borsa di New York – alle 15:30 ora italiana – le azioni di Anthropic inizieranno a essere negoziate sul mercato (e nello specifico al Nasdaq, il listino dei titoli tecnologici). Visto il grande entusiasmo per questa quotazione, con ogni probabilità il prezzo salirà ancora per la grande richiesta degli investitori, così anche il valore dell’intera società.

Il prezzo iniziale è comunque già superiore alle stime: la scorsa settimana la società aveva indicato un intervallo compreso tra 70 e 78 dollari per azione, ma le tante richieste degli investitori hanno portato su il prezzo. Per dimensioni, l’IPO supera quella di SpaceX, l’azienda spaziale e di comunicazioni satellitari di Elon Musk, che a giugno aveva raccolto 75 miliardi di dollari dagli investitori. Al momento della quotazione però SpaceX aveva una valutazione complessiva più alta: 1.770 miliardi di dollari.

Quella di Anthropic è una valutazione enorme per un’azienda nata appena cinque anni fa e che ancora non produce utili, anzi: dagli ultimi dati disponibili, nei primi nove mesi del 2026 ha registrato una perdita operativa di 1,3 miliardi di dollari. La perdita operativa mostra cosa si ottiene se dai ricavi si sottraggono i costi, ed è quindi l’indicatore che più mostra come va un’azienda nel suo business principale; secondo le regole contabili statunitensi però la perdita è persino più ampia, 104 miliardi di dollari, se si considerano particolari strumenti finanziari che, senza entrare troppo nei dettagli, l’azienda ha emesso per finanziare le sue attività ma che contribuiscono ad allargare il disavanzo.

Ciononostante Anthropic sta crescendo. Nei primi 9 mesi dell’anno ha ottenuto ricavi per 33 miliardi di dollari, molto superiori rispetto ai 4,6 miliardi di tutto il 2025. Il problema principale è se e quando questa crescita riuscirà a portare l’azienda a essere profittevole.

Un’altra particolarità della quotazione di Anthropic riguarda il poco potere decisionale che avranno le persone che ne compreranno le azioni, ovvero i futuri azionisti. In genere nelle aziende gli azionisti partecipano all’elezione dei membri del consiglio di amministrazione, l’organo che definisce le strategie di sviluppo societario. Anthropic, invece, ha creato una struttura organizzativa per cui gli azionisti avranno un potere molto limitato. Avviene lo stesso in altre aziende tecnologiche statunitensi.

La quotazione arriva in un momento delicato per le società del settore: la vittoria del Partito Democratico alle elezioni di metà mandato ha fatto aumentare tra gli investitori i timori di una maggiore regolamentazione, specialmente nello sviluppo dei data center; i recenti scandali che hanno coinvolto l’ex amministratore delegato di Nvidia Jensen Huang hanno creato problemi a una delle società più importanti del settore, col rischio che si espandano ad altre aziende; e da tempo molti osservatori si chiedono se non sia in corso una bolla speculativa.

L’andamento della quotazione di Anthropic è insomma un modo per analizzare a che punto è la maturazione del settore delle intelligenze artificiali e che valutazione ne danno analisti e investitori. Sarà inoltre osservato attentamente da OpenAI, l’azienda del chatbot ChatGPT e rivale di Anthropic, la cui quotazione dovrebbe avvenire nei prossimi mesi.

articles.title: Malaysia leads Southeast Asia’s IPO race, but analysts warn post-listing performance is the real test
articles.summary: While Malaysia dominated Southeast Asia’s IPO market in the first nine months of 2026 with 38 of the region's 56 listings, analysts caution that over half of this year’s debutants are trading underwater.
articles.preview: While Malaysia dominated Southeast Asia’s IPO market in the first nine months of 2026 with 38 of the region's 56 listings, analysts caution that over half of this year’s debutants are trading underwater. KUALA LUMPUR: Defying a broader regional slowdown, Malaysia has emerged as the engine of Southeast Asia’s initial public offering (IPO) market in 2026.
articles.body:
While Malaysia dominated Southeast Asia’s IPO market in the first nine months of 2026 with 38 of the region's 56 listings, analysts caution that over half of this year’s debutants are trading underwater.

KUALA LUMPUR: Defying a broader regional slowdown, Malaysia has emerged as the engine of Southeast Asia’s initial public offering (IPO) market in 2026.

According to global accounting and consulting firm Ernst & Young (EY), Malaysia’s bourse operator, Bursa Malaysia, captured more than two-thirds - or 38 of 56 - of all regional listings in the first nine months of the year.

Total proceeds - the amount of money raised by companies listed on the stock exchange - surged 63 per cent to US$1.62billion in the first nine months of the year, compared to US$992 million over the same period last year.

E&Y said ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and uncertainty about near-term prospects had led IPO aspirants in the region to take a more cautious approach with their listing plans, but Malaysia had bucked that trend.

While headline listing numbers and fundraising totals put Malaysia firmly ahead of regional peers, analysts cautioned that listing volume alone does not guarantee investor returns or long-term market competitiveness.

Loui Low, the head of research at Malaysian stockbroker M+Global, said that while Malaysia’s IPO momentum is encouraging, success should be measured by post-listing performance rather than listing numbers.

“Quality over quantity will be crucial to sustaining investor confidence and attracting long-term capital,” he told CNA.

WHY MALAYSIA HAS PULLED AHEAD

Nghia Trung Nguyen, of Ernst & Young’s capital markets division, told CNA that Malaysia has maintained a robust listing pipeline - particularly on the ACE Market - underpinned by deep domestic liquidity, referring to how much money is available within a country from large domestic investors and financial institutions to invest in its financial markets.

The Main Market caters to larger, established corporations, while the ACE Market serves as a stepping stone for smaller and mid-sized firms.

“This momentum also reflects the role of the capital market in supporting companies as they pursue their next phase of growth, providing access to capital while broadening their investor base and market profile,” said Nghia.

He said that the technology, construction, healthcare and consumer businesses continue to attract interest, while the ACE Market provides an accessible fundraising platform.

Over the past year, high-profile Main Market debutants have included integrated circuit designer SkyeChip and private hospital operator Sunway Healthcare Holdings, while the ACE Market continued to anchor overall listing volume with high-growth small and mid-sized enterprises.

Of the 38 listings, six were in the main market, and 32 were in the ACE Market.

Economist Sedek Jantan of IPP, a financial planning group in Malaysia, attributed Malaysia's performance to three main factors: the depth of domestic institutional liquidity, an appealing market setup for raising funds, and upbeat stock market conditions driving companies to bring forward their listings.

He said that local institutions such as Malaysia’s pension fund - the Employees Provident Fund (EPF) - and Permodalan Nasional Berhad (PNB) - Malaysia's largest state-owned investment fund - provide a substantial pool of domestic savings that can be channelled into the capital market.

“This creates an important foundation for IPO demand, particularly for larger offerings where institutional participation is essential,” he said.

PNB has RM365.3 billion (US$89.2 billion) in assets, while the EPF has total investment assets of RM1.54 trillion, roughly 61 per cent of which is invested in domestic markets, and 39 per cent is invested in international markets.

While local institutional funds helped sustain deal flow in Kuala Lumpur, regional peers faced tougher challenges.

By contrast, Indonesia saw a sharp pullback to just seven listings, raising US$121.3million, down from 23 IPOs worth US$919.6 million a year earlier, while Thailand’s tally fell from eight to three listings, with proceeds more than halving to US$21.3 million from US$57.6 million.

Singapore, meanwhile, logged eight listings, one more than a year earlier, although total funds raised dipped to US$1.28 billion from US$1.54 billion.

THE REALITY CHECK

However, observers stressed that while Malaysia is demonstrating strength in IPO accessibility and fundraising activity, it was not established that this translated into superior capital-market depth, issuer quality and long-term competitiveness.

They pointed out that performance of the companies has been mixed, with a wide gap between the strongest and weakest listings.

Loui said that with more than half of this year’s Main and ACE Market IPOs trading below issue prices, investors should prioritise fundamentals over listing-day excitement.

He said that as of Nov 4, only 46 per cent of the 46 Main and ACE Market IPOs were trading above their issue prices, while 54 per cent were underwater.

“This highlights that strong IPO demand does not necessarily translate into sustainable returns,” he said.

Nghia said this underscored the importance of companies delivering on the growth story presented at IPO and sustaining investor confidence beyond the listing.

“Strong oversubscription or a first-day gain is not a reliable guide to longer-term returns,” he said.

“There is always a risk of companies rushing to market when sentiment is positive, but an IPO is really just the start of being a public company. Companies need to ensure their valuation is realistic, their governance, financial reporting and controls are ready, and their growth story remains credible after listing,” he added.

Sedek echoed this view and said that companies tended to accelerate their listing decisions during periods of strong equity-market performance, favourable valuations and elevated investor optimism.

“Companies are effectively making a financing decision based on the relative cost of equity capital,” he said, adding that he would not interpret Malaysia's strong IPO performance as definitive evidence that the country’s capital market has become structurally more competitive.

He said that companies should not rush to list simply because market conditions are favourable but because their businesses are ready to become publicly accountable and because the capital raised can generate meaningful future returns.

He added that Malaysia needed to move from a liquidity-supported IPO market towards an internationally competitive, investor-driven capital market.

He said this meant attracting foreign institutional investors based on the quality of companies, strengthening research coverage and improving corporate governance, rather than relying predominantly on domestic institutional demand.

“When EPF or PNB subscribes to a Malaysian IPO, the investment may simply represent a reallocation of existing domestic savings from one financial asset into another. It does not necessarily represent additional capital entering the Malaysian economy,” he added.

articles.body:
As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

articles.body:
L’azienda è stata selezionata da Trungnam Group per la commessa destinata al progetto Cà Ná Lng, una struttura da 1.500 megawatt

Ansaldo Energia rafforza la sua presenza in Vietnam. L’azienda genovese è stata selezionata da Trungnam Group per la fornitura di due turbine a gas e due generatori destinati al progetto Cà Ná Lng , una nuova centrale elettrica da 1.500 megawatt che sarà realizzata nel Vietnam centrale. L’accordo è stato firmato oggi a Ho Chi Minh City. La centrale Cà Ná Lng è inclusa nel Revised power development plan VIII del Paese, il piano nazionale che guida lo sviluppo del sistema elettrico vietnamita, e contribuirà a soddisfare la crescente domanda di energia elettrica.

Una volta operativa, spiega una nota, la centrale produrrà circa 9 terawattora di energia elettrica l’anno destinati alla rete nazionale. Al centro del nuovo impianto ci sarà la GT36 di Ansaldo Energia, turbina a gas di punta dell’azienda. La consegna delle due turbine a gas e dei due generatori è prevista nel 2029, in linea con l’obiettivo del progetto di raggiungere l’operatività commerciale entro la fine del 2030.

«Il progetto Cà Ná - afferma Stefano Gianatti, Executive vice president thermal new units di Ansaldo - rappresenta un passo importante nel rafforzamento della nostra presenza in Vietnam e in Asia. Con l’espansione della capacità di generazione elettrica del Vietnam a sostegno della crescita economica, il sistema avrà sempre più bisogno di una generazione affidabile e flessibile. La GT36 è particolarmente adatta a rispondere a queste esigenze, grazie alla combinazione di efficienza e flessibilità operativa».

articles.title: US: Protesters warn of AI bubble as Anthropic makes stock market history
articles.summary: Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut with a record-breaking IPO valuing the AI company at $1.5 trillion. Outside the exchange in New York, police detained three protesters warning of financial risks.

articles.body: Priced at $83 a share, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot raised over $80 billion and achieved a $1.5 trillion valuation on its Wall Street debut. Inside Nasdaq, co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the opening bell to celebrate the start of trading; outside, protesters chanted against the flotation and the concentration of tech-sector wealth in a demonstration that saw three people detained by police. The listing overtook SpaceX’s blockbuster June offering, highlighting relentless investor enthusiasm for AI despite growing talk of overheated technology valuations. Robust demand carried the share price clear of its earlier $70 to $78 guide range. Yet demonstrators warned that ordinary investors could pay the price if the AI surge ends in a financial bust. Jose Gonzalez, among those protesting outside, questioned who would bear the brunt of a market reversal, arguing that wealthy investors enjoy protections unavailable to the public. The meteoric surge of artificial intelligence is sparking hope and alarm in equal measure. While global spending on AI approaches $850 billion in 2026 and enthusiasts hail a sweeping economic and technological revolution, economists and watchdogs warn of a looming financial bubble, swelling debt and growing inequality, alongside fears that automation will wipe out jobs and funnel vast wealth into the coffers of a few tech titans.
